questions.question: What is the main limitation of a standard digital certificate (e.g., X.509) when used for selective attribute disclosure?
options: The verifier sees all attributes even if they only need one, and every presentation is linkable via the signature
X.509 certificates cannot be verified offline without contacting the issuer
X.509 uses symmetric keys so the holder cannot prove ownership
The certificate size grows linearly with the number of attributes, making it too large
questions.explanation: Traditional certificates expose all attributes and use a fixed signature, so every presentation leaks the same data and can be tracked by colluding verifiers.

questions.question: In a BBS+ credential, what does the 'A' component of the signature represent?
options: A = B^(1/(e+sk)) mod p — a compressed representation of all messages bound under the issuer key
A = G^sk mod p — the issuer's public key
A = H(messages) — a hash commitment to all attributes
A = e + sk mod p — the signature scalar used in verification
questions.explanation: A is the BBS+ 'certificate' element computed from the message commitment B raised to the inverse of (e+sk). Verification checks A^(e+sk) == B.

questions.question: Why does production BBS+ verification use a bilinear pairing e(A, W·G^e) == e(B, G) instead of checking A^(e+sk) == B?
options: The pairing lets the verifier check the equation without knowing sk, so the issuer secret key never needs to be shared
The pairing is faster than modular exponentiation for large exponents
The pairing eliminates the need for a public key entirely
The pairing makes the proof zero-knowledge by hiding the value of A
questions.explanation: The pairing equation binds the issuer public key W = G^sk into the check algebraically. Knowing W (not sk) is enough to verify, which is the whole point of a public-key signature scheme.

questions.question: In the selective disclosure proof, how does the verifier reconstruct B without seeing hidden messages?
options: The prover supplies H_i^{m_i} (partial commitments) for each hidden attribute, allowing B to be reconstructed from revealed values plus these commitments
The verifier queries the issuer database to fill in missing attribute values
The prover reveals a hash of hidden attributes and the verifier uses it to reconstruct B
B is sent directly in the proof; the verifier only needs to check the signature on B
questions.explanation: Each hidden attribute m_i is replaced by its generator commitment H_i^{m_i}. The verifier multiplies revealed generator terms and hidden commitments to get the same B that the issuer signed.

questions.question: What property does the full BBS+ protocol achieve that this toy implementation does NOT?
options: Unlinkability: each presentation randomises A so different verifiers cannot correlate proofs from the same credential
Selective disclosure: revealing only a subset of signed attributes without re-signing
Issuer binding: proving the credential came from a specific issuer key
Multi-message signing: covering all attributes with a single compact signature
questions.explanation: The toy passes the same (A, e, s) every time. Full BBS+ randomises A per presentation via a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge, making presentations unlinkable.

questions.question: An attacker intercepts a BBS+ selective disclosure proof and replays it to a second verifier. Which mechanism prevents this?
options: The verifier supplies a fresh nonce that is bound into the proof; replaying to a different verifier fails because the nonce won't match
BBS+ signatures include a timestamp that expires after one use
The issuer revokes the credential after the first presentation is detected
The holder's public key is included and checked against a live registry on every presentation
questions.explanation: Each verifier generates a fresh nonce and requires it to be included in the proof. A replayed proof carries the old nonce and fails the freshness check.

questions.question: In this toy implementation, bbs_verify requires the issuer secret key sk. What is the practical consequence of this design?
options: Verification cannot be done by a third party without the issuer sharing sk, which breaks the security model of a public-key scheme
Only the issuer can verify signatures, which is acceptable for credential auditing
The holder can forge signatures since they need sk to verify their own credential
sk must be included in the credential so the holder can verify it
questions.explanation: In a real scheme the verifier should only need the public key. Requiring sk means the issuer must share secrets with every verifier — exactly the problem bilinear pairings were designed to solve.

questions.question: Why are production BBS+ generators chosen as hash-to-curve outputs rather than simple powers of G (as in this toy)?
options: Hash-to-curve generators have no known discrete log relationship to each other, preventing a holder from constructing a commitment for one slot that is also valid for another slot
Hash-to-curve generators are faster to compute than repeated squaring
Hash-to-curve ensures generators are on the correct side of a Type-3 pairing
Powers of G would make the public key derivable from any generator
questions.explanation: If H_i = G^i, then pow(H_i, m, P) == pow(G, i*m, P) and attribute slots are algebraically related. Hash-to-curve removes these known relations, hardening the binding of each message to its dedicated slot.
